items.title: [DRAFT] Adds latency-optimized, redux-based reduce-then-scan algorithm
items.body:
### Open questions:

- Naming and fallback behavior: We use a fallback if redux is not supported (i.e.,`detail::is_warp_redux_op_supported`). I am semi-happy with the current choice of `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_REDUCE_THEN_SCAN`, as it sounds that we'd always reduce-then-scan. I wonder if (a) we should change the name to something like `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_REDUX_THEN_SCAN` or if we should even consider changing the fallback behaviour to _always_ perform a reduce-then-scan. 

### Eligibility and fallback

This PR adds a new, opt-in `BlockScanAlgorithm`. It is a warp-granularity "reduce-then-scan" variant of `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_SCANS` that minimizes the time until the block aggregate (and with it, a `BlockPrefixCallbackOp`) becomes available.

It also fits the existing naming scheme: `BLOCK_SCAN_RAKING` is reduce-then-scan done by sequential raking in a single warp, this variant is reduce-then-scan done by hardware warp reductions with all warps active, and `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_SCANS` is scan-then-propagate.

### Where the latency goes today

Every thread's result needs two independent ingredients: its warp-local prefix (a scan over its warp's 32 inputs) and its warp base (the sum of the preceding warps' aggregates). `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_SCANS` computes them one after the other, because each warp's aggregate only exists as a by-product of its scan (the last lane's inclusive value):

```text
LDS(~33) -> 5-shuffle scan (~150) -> aggregate now known -> store -> BARRIER -> fold aggregates (~63) -> result
            \_______________________________________________________/
            the aggregate exchange is welded to the END of the scan chain
```

This has two structural costs. The barrier releases late, since a warp only arrives once its full shuffle chain is done. And the cross-warp fold turns into a serial tail: its loads can't be hoisted above the barrier, and by the time it runs, every warp has already finished its scan, so there is nothing left to overlap it with.

### What this variant changes

`redux.sync` produces a warp's aggregate in about 22 cycles without any scan, which decouples the two ingredients:

```text
LDS(~33) -> redux(~22) -> store -> BARRIER (releases ~120 cycles earlier)
                                    |-> 5-shuffle scan (~150)     unchanged, each warp's own work
                                    |-> fold aggregates (~63)     independent LDS/adds, issued in the
                                                                  shuffle chain's stall slots
                                 -> result  (join: incl + base)
```

The scan itself is not any faster. The point is that nothing queues up behind it anymore. The fold's loads and adds don't depend on the shuffles, so the SASS scheduler interleaves them into the shuffle chain's stall cycles (about 14 issue slots hidden in about 120 stall cycles). Wall time after the barrier becomes max(scan, fold) instead of scan + barrier wait + fold. In the prefix-callback overloads, warp 0 additionally invokes the callback right after the fold and before its own scan, so the callback's latency (typically global memory) also hides under the other warps' scans.

### Eligibility and fallback

Results are identical to `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_SCANS`. Eligibility (`detail::is_warp_redux_op_supported`) is limited to associative, commutative integer operators (sum/min/max/bitwise, types up to 4 bytes), where the redux-computed aggregate is bit-exact. Unsupported operators/types and pre-sm_80 targets fall back to the classic code paths at compile/dispatch time. Blocks that aren't a multiple of the warp size fall back to raking via `SAFE_ALGORITHM`, same as `BLOCK_SCAN_WARP_SCANS`. `TempStorage` is unchanged: it reuses the `BlockScanWarpScans` layout, including the existing `warp_aggregates` array. The variant only changes who writes that array, and when.

### Results and scope

Measured on B200 (sm_100), callback-style `int` exclusive sum, 256 threads, single resident block: 397 -> 320 cycles/call, a 19.5% reduction. The motivating use case is latency-critical block-scope primitives where the scan sits on a pass-serial critical path with no other resident work to hide stalls. Concretely: the radix pass of block-level top-k selection, where this stage is about 40% of the optimized call and the change saves 64 to 82 cycles per pass.

Scope note: I also tried routing a decoupled look-back algorithm (`DeviceSelect`) through this variant and found no measurable end-to-end change on B200. Presumably, the windowed look-back absorbs the earlier aggregate publication. This will require further investigation. The main target for now, is `BlockTopK`.

## Checklist

- [x] New specialization `detail::BlockScanWarpReduceThenScan` (full method surface, compile-time and runtime fallback)
- [x] Enum value, docs, `to_string`, and `InternalBlockScan` dispatch in `block_scan.cuh`
- [x] Added to the catch2 `BlockScan` test algorithm matrix
- [x] Validated on sm_100: exclusive/inclusive, single/multi-item, with/without aggregate, multi-tile prefix callback; eligible and fallback paths against host references

items.title: Add Numba-CUDA-MLIR Block Load and Store to cuda.coop
items.body:
## Why this is needed

This adds the first executable `cuda.coop` capability for
Numba-CUDA-MLIR: cooperative Block Load and Block Store. It establishes a
portable API contract and a registry-driven compiler seam that later
primitive families can extend without adding family-specific logic to
activation, root dispatch, caching, header discovery, or phase orchestration.

The qualified API mirrors the portable names, defaults, dtype inference, and
lowercase string selectors. For this slice, its only additional payload option
is `ThreadData(..., alignas=...)` for compiler-specific alignment.

## Reviewer-visible behavior

- Lowers CUB BlockLoad and BlockStore with `algorithm="direct"` for
  `this_block()`, including 1D/2D/3D launches, scalar and multi-item Store,
  partial tiles, offsets, and Load defaults.
- Uses the source or destination array dtype as the inference authority.
  Portable and qualified `ThreadData` may both omit `dtype`.
- Requires runtime arrays and compiler scalars to match the payload dtype
  exactly. Ordinary Python literals are contextually checked for type and
  range before provider generation.
- Tracks runtime scalar provenance through kernel arguments, CUDA indices,
  array elements, casts, expressions, aliases, and phi nodes.
- Carries runtime `valid_items` through a signed 64-bit ABI and traps before
  narrowing when it is outside
  `0 <= valid_items <= group_size * items_per_thread`. Grid-stride tail counts
  must therefore be clamped by the caller.
- Makes DIRECT Load and Store storage-free in both the portable plan and
  compiler backend. Providers use CUB's default constructor and emit no
  backing allocation, pointer argument, or reuse barrier.
- Accepts explicit shared, exclusive, sized, unsized, or dynamic
  `TempStorage` descriptors for DIRECT calls as validated but unused
  descriptors; they do not affect plan or artifact identity.
- Keeps `ThreadGroup` descriptor-only. Group construction and hierarchy
  descriptors remain planning vocabulary, while standalone rank, count,
  synchronization, and membership methods remain out of scope.
- Discovers both monolithic CUDA 13 installations and CUDA 12 split-wheel
  layouts containing headers, NVRTC plus builtins, and nvJitLink.

The portable and qualified kernel flow is intentionally symmetric:

```python
block = coop.this_block()
items = coop.ThreadData(2)
coop.load(
    block,
    source,
    items,
    algorithm="direct",
    offset=cuda.blockIdx.x * TILE,
)
coop.store(
    block,
    destination,
    items,
    algorithm="direct",
    offset=cuda.blockIdx.x * TILE,
)
```

Computed Store values still require an explicit cast when Numba promotes an
expression, for example `types.int32(index + 1)` for an `int32` destination.

## Architecture and compatibility

Provider metadata declares result provenance, dtype keywords, namespaces,
storage ABI, execution scope, synchronization scope, and scalar parameter
ABIs. Planning and rewrite hooks receive bounded interfaces, and the generic
adapter consumes registered declarations without recognizing Load, Store, or
family-specific parameter names.

Activation is transactional and idempotent. Private Numba-CUDA-MLIR registry,
overload, datamodel, compiler-IR, and supported-version access is confined to
one guarded compatibility module for `numba-cuda-mlir>=0.5,<0.6`. This shim is
accepted follow-up debt until an upstream public extension API is available.

Supported activation orders are Numba first followed by the portable API, or
`cuda.coop` first followed by an explicitly aliased import:

```python
import cuda.coop.numba_mlir as _coop_numba_mlir
```

A bare dotted import after `from numba_cuda_mlir import cuda` would rebind the
local `cuda` name. Root first followed only by Numba remains unsupported and
produces the documented `Unknown attribute 'this_block'` diagnostic.

## Validation

- An exact-head wheel built from
  `942180485ee497e79cc3d652478163e7552455bb` was installed outside the source
  tree.
- The installed wheel passed 274 contract, packaging, public-surface, and
  activation tests under `python -P`.
- The exact head passed 489 GPU-hidden backend unit and compile tests.
- All 57 focused runtime tests passed on an RTX PRO 6000, including
  grid-stride tails, divergent DIRECT calls, caller descriptors, dynamic
  storage validation, and isolated invalid-runtime traps.
- Changed-file pre-commit and `git diff --check` passed.

## Scope and qualification boundary

Reduce, Scan, concrete Warp primitives, CUDAX dispatch, callbacks, and Python
operator compilation remain outside this foundation PR.

CUDA 12/13 L4 and Windows CI remain external readiness gates. This PR remains
a draft until those lanes and reviewer feedback are complete.

items.title: [FEA]: Using `thrust::device` execution policy in device code should fail to compile

labels.name: thrust
labels.description: For all items related to Thrust.

type.name: Enhancement
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
### Is this a duplicate?

- [X] I confirmed there appear to be no [duplicate issues](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/issues) for this request and that I agree to the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Area

Thrust

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

As a user of Thrust, I might want to use a Thrust algorithm within the body of a kernel. Whether intentional or accidental, I might try and use the `thrust::device` execution policy. For example,

```
__global__
void kernel(...){
   auto result = thrust::reduce(thrust::device, ....);
}
```

What should I expect actually happens here? 

#### Context: CUDA Dynamic Parallelism (CDP)

The answer is complicated and relates to breaking changes that happened with CUDA Dynamic Parallelism (CDP) with the introduction of sm_90.

In short, prior to sm_90, you could do the following:
```
__global__ void CDPv1_kernel(){
   kernel<<<...>>>(...); // device side launch, aka CDP
   cudaDeviceSynchronize(); // This is the important piece
}
```
In other words, you could launch a child kernel, and then synchronize to wait for the results from that kernel. This is know as "CDPv1".

CDPv1 was [deprecated in CUDA 11.6 ](https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cuda-c-programming-guide/index.html#dynamic-parallelism-synchronization) and removed in CUDA 12.0.

You can still launch child kernels, but you can no longer block and synchronize to wait for their results. This is known as **CDPv2**. The recommended practice instead of synchronizing is to launch an additional tail child kernel that consumes the result of the first child kernel. 

```
__global__ void CDPv1_kernel(){
   kernel<<<...>>>(result,...); // device side launch, aka CDP
   // cudaDeviceSynchronize(); // Can't do this
   tail_kernel<<<...>>>(result...) // need to do this
}
```

#### CDPv1, CDPv2 and Thrust

To understand how this relates to Thrust, one must first understand that Thrust algorithms are inherently synchronous. Consider `thrust::reduce` that returns its result. It needs to synchronize the work of the kernel in order to ensure the final result is available. 

In CDPv1, using `thrust::reduce(thrust::device,...` in a kernel would launch a child kernel and synchronize before returning the result. 

With CDPv2, this is no longer possible. Therefore, it is not possible to preserve Thrust algorithm's synchronous semantics with CDPv2.

This would mean any existing code using `thrust::device` in device code would break. To avoid breaking that code, a decision was made to make `thrust::device` implicitly fallback to `thrust::seq`, i.e., it no longer launches a child kernel and instead just runs sequentially on the calling thread.  

We have since realized that this was a mistake for two main reasons:
1. It is too astonishing to users
2. It is too onerous to maintain 


### Describe the solution you'd like

Using a Thrust algorithm with the `thrust::device` execution policy should fail to compile and emit a helpful diagnostic explaining why and directing the user to use `thrust::seq` instead if that's the behavior they want. 

### Describe alternatives you've considered

An alternative would be to develop a more asynchronous programming model for Thrust where algorithms don't need to synchronize. `thrust::async` was a little known and undocumented attempt at doing this, but was quickly abandoned and we have no plans to revive it. 

Furthermore, some algorithms don't _really_ need to synchronize because they don't return a result. This is part of the reason why we added the [`thrust::cuda::par_nosync`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/blob/0ff0f61c02c38c2ca25b92db06ff49a75140ca1f/thrust/examples/cuda/explicit_cuda_stream.cu#L40-L50) execution policy. But this execution policy is merely a _hint_. Some algorithms still require synchronization to be functionally correct.

We could explore adding a new execution policy similar to `thrust::cuda::par_nosync` that is only allowed on algorithms that truly do not need to synchronize. This could then be used for device-side usage of Thrust algorithms where launching a child kernel is desired.

However, all of this is purely hypothetical and we currently have no plans to explore it. There would need to be considerable demands from users for this kind of functionality for us to seriously consider investing time into exploring this. 

### Additional context

For the record, CUB algorithms _do_ work with CDPv2 because CUB's programming model is asynchronous and more akin to launching a kernel directly. If someone truly wanted device-side kernel launch, then using an equivalent CUB algorithm would be the best way to do it.

items.title: [cub] Add cooperative cached high-bin histograms
items.body:
## Why When a histogram is too large for block-private shared memory, the existing implementation gives every block a complete private histogram in global memory and performs a separate gather afterward. That is robust, but it initializes, updates, and gathers a large amount of global memory. This PR adds the high-bin algorithm selected by the autoresearch work. Each block still owns a private global-memory histogram, but a shared-memory cache absorbs repeated updates. Cache misses are run-length encoded before they update the private histogram, and a cooperative grid gathers the private histograms directly into the output after a grid-wide barrier. The low-bin algorithms are deliberately unchanged. PR #10556 owns static and runtime-sized shared-memory privatization. ## What changed - Add a cooperative histogram kernel with configurable cache, spill, and aggregation strategies. - Use the winning production configuration on SM100: single-probe shared-memory cache, block-private global-memory spill, RLE-compressed misses, and cooperative gather. - Validate the policy-selected cache size against the selected kernel's dynamic-shared-memory and occupancy limits. - Keep separate ordinary and high-bin transforms, so optimized EVEN and RANGE classification does not alter the existing low-bin or fallback kernels. - Use 32-bit local/cache counters when the final output counter is wider, widening only when contributions are written to the output. - Add staged single-channel loading and vectorized, classify-before-probe multi-channel loading. - Add policy, dispatch-boundary, launcher, correctness, and fallback coverage. All algorithm and tuning choices are part of the existing `HistogramPolicy`; there is no parallel policy hierarchy. ## Dispatch ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Histogram request] --> B{Histogram is in the high-bin tier?} B -- No --> C[Existing low-bin or fallback path] B -- Yes --> D{Host launch and cooperative launch supported?} D -- No --> C D -- Yes --> E[Select high-bin policy] E --> F[Validate the policy cache against
the kernel's dynamic-SMEM and occupancy limits] F --> G{At least one cooperative block
can reside on every SM?} G -- No --> C G -- Yes --> H[Launch cooperative grid] H --> I[Initialize output and block-private histograms] I --> J[Load and classify samples] J --> K{Single-probe cache hit?} K -- Yes --> L[Update replicated shared-memory counter] K -- No --> M[RLE-compress misses and update
the block-private global histogram] L --> N[Flush cache to the private histogram] M --> N N --> O[Grid-wide barrier] O --> P[Cooperatively gather private histograms
into the output] ``` On SM100 with 32-bit local counters, the production high-bin boundaries match the raw autoresearch selector: - single-channel EVEN and RANGE: above the 228,352-byte on-chip capacity; the first swept high-bin point is 57,344 bins; - three-active-channel EVEN: above the same total capacity; the first swept high-bin point is 32,768 bins; - three-active-channel RANGE: above the measured 8,192-byte-per-channel crossover; the first swept high-bin point is 4,096 bins. For example, three-active-channel EVEN at 16,384 bins is intentionally not a high-bin comparison. The raw branch runs its runtime-sized shared-memory kernel there, while this independent PR leaves the existing trunk path unchanged. A controlled PR-versus-trunk check across 15 shapes and six element counts measured 0.99997x geometric mean, with a 0.991x minimum and 1.002x maximum. ## Performance versus the raw autoresearch winner The final B200 sweep compares production source `3fa42516e4ca1a5c1b0cba49f3d7766d314ce0e7` with raw autoresearch winner `27edbac6ec2799cf1fe887312d6202c108cfa3b6`. The benchmark-only input generators and the run and graph scripts are taken from the raw branch. The selector is unforced on both sides. Coverage: - single-channel EVEN and RANGE, plus four-channel/three-active-channel EVEN and RANGE; - I32 and F64 samples; - 32-bit and 64-bit output-counter builds; - only bins where the raw selector and this PR both select the cooperative high-bin algorithm: 57,344 through 1,048,576 for single-channel, 32,768 through 1,048,576 for multi-channel EVEN, and 4,096 through 1,048,576 for multi-channel RANGE; - 1M, 16M, 64M, 256M, 1G, and 2B elements; - all 15 autoresearch input shapes; - three samples per cell with a 20 ms minimum measurement time. This is 5,580 matched cells per output-counter build, or 11,160 total. | API | sample | 32-bit output PR/raw | 64-bit output PR/raw | worst measured cell | |---|---|---:|---:|---:| | single-channel EVEN | I32 | **1.013x** | **1.014x** | 0.920x | | single-channel EVEN | F64 | **1.007x** | **1.005x** | 0.897x | | single-channel RANGE | I32 | **1.119x** | **1.118x** | 0.866x | | single-channel RANGE | F64 | **1.052x** | **1.053x** | 0.757x | | three-active-channel EVEN | I32 | **1.017x** | **1.016x** | 0.874x | | three-active-channel EVEN | F64 | **1.012x** | **1.012x** | 0.880x | | three-active-channel RANGE | I32 | **1.042x** | **1.047x** | 0.741x | | three-active-channel RANGE | F64 | **1.055x** | **1.063x** | 0.814x | | **all high-bin cells** | | **1.039x** | **1.041x** | **0.741x** | The production port matches or slightly exceeds the raw winner in aggregate for every API/sample/output-counter combination. It is not pointwise identical: the remaining tails are concentrated in `hash_synonym`, small 4,096-bin multi-channel RANGE inputs, and a few large stale-resident cases. Repeated, order-controlled reruns confirmed those are real code-generation/launch-shape tradeoffs rather than timing order. A lower-register launch-bound experiment improved the hash-heavy tail but caused much larger stale-resident regressions, so it was not adopted. ### 32-bit output counters ![Single-channel EVEN I32](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/even_single_I32/all_geomean.png) ![Single-channel EVEN F64](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/even_single_F64/all_geomean.png) ![Single-channel RANGE I32](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/range_single_I32/all_geomean.png) ![Single-channel RANGE F64](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/range_single_F64/all_geomean.png) ![Three-active-channel EVEN I32](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/even_multi_I32/all_geomean.png) ![Three-active-channel EVEN F64](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/even_multi_F64/all_geomean.png) ![Three-active-channel RANGE I32](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/range_multi_I32/all_geomean.png) ![Three-active-channel RANGE F64](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/robobryce/cccl/34c9dff0b0/pr-assets/10568/comprehensive/c32/range_multi_F64/all_geomean.png) ### 64-bit output counters

items.body:
### Is this a duplicate?

- [x] I confirmed there appear to be no [duplicate issues](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/issues) for this request and that I agree to the [Code of Conduct](CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md)

### Area

CUB

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Currently, CUB::SegmentedSort uses a coarse-grained small/medium/large strategy for binning segment lengths. Due to the coarseness of the binning, a significant amount wasted work is performed when an input's distribution of segment lengths is far from the maximum size of a bin, significantly decreasing performance. This problem cannot be solved by library-level tuning, as changing the size of a bin increases performance for some segment  lengths at the cost of others.

### Describe the solution you'd like

There are two avenues of granularity which should be explored:

Kernel Level Granularity: Investigate the performance impact of increasing granularity to the [logarithmic radix binning](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/8547581) scheme used by [Hou et al.](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/3079079.3079105), [Kobus et al.](https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1007/978-3-031-39698-4_45), and [GPUSorting](https://github.com/b0nes164/GPUSorting/tree/cleanup/GPUSortingCUDA/SegSort/SplitSort). While increasing kernel granularity improves performance by reducing wasted work, it also risks higher kernel launch overheads and occupancy tail costs. Although the current CUB use model precludes multiple cudaStreams, PDL could potentially enable concurrent kernel execution; this is currently being investigated in #6790.

Dynamic/Runtime Granularity: Investigate the impact of dynamically choosing size-specialized algorithm variants within a kernel. For algorithms that are generally threadblock uniform, this should always yield a performance increase. For algorithms that aren't, dynamically branching on segment length increases efficiency at the risk of thrashing the instruction cache, so the advantage is less clear.

### Describe alternatives you've considered

_No response_

### Additional context

An issue with existing  implementations of  "fine-grain" segmented sort is that histogramming during the binning pass is done by atomics. This creates an unstable ordering of segments within the bin, which can cause cache locality/memory access inefficiencies in the downstream sort.

The solution to this is to replace pure atomic histogramming with a multisplit/warp_match_any based approach. This preserves a stable ordering of segments, and because the number of bins is typically less than 16, only 4 bits are required to match on, ensuring low ALU overhead during the multisplit/warp_match_any.

Functionally, this kernel would operate almost identically to a single round of OneSweep sort.

     - Introduce new agent template parameter `MaxSegmentsPerBlock` which controls the size of `OffsetT` array in shared memory dedicated to storing inclusive-scan of segment sizes. The actual number of segments to process is passed dynamically to `consume_ranges` method. It can not exceed `MaxSegmentsPerBlock`, however.

items.title: Add `cuda::bit_fns` to `<cuda/bit>`
items.body:
## Summary

Adds `cuda::bit_fns` to `<cuda/bit>`.

The implementation generalizes the binary-search algorithm currently used by CUB's
run-length encoder (`cub/device/dispatch/kernels/kernel_rle_encode_lookahead.cuh`,
`nth_set_bit`) to all supported unsigned integer types, as requested in #11051. That
helper carries a `TODO (Nan): as per discussion with Federico, this could be in
libcudacxx`; this PR is that move. It does not yet replace the CUB call site.

## Semantics

`bit_fns(value, rank)` returns the zero-based position of the zero-based `rank`-th
set bit of `value`, counting from the least significant bit. The return type is
`int`, since the result is a position. If `value` has fewer than `rank + 1` set bits
the result is `-1`, that is `0xFFFFFFFF`, the not-found result of the `__fns`
intrinsic.

The only precondition is `0 <= rank && rank < num_bits(T)`, checked with
`_CCCL_ASSERT` as in `bitmask` and `bitfield_insert`. A zero `value` is inside the
contract and yields `-1` for every rank.

## Implementation

The not-found case is an early exit. After it, each of the `log2(num_bits(T))` steps
counts the set bits in the low half of the remaining window with `popcount`; if the
wanted rank is not among them the low half is discarded, the rank is reduced by that
count, and the position advances by the half width. The loop invariant is that the
accumulated position is the offset of the current window in the original value and
the remaining rank is the index of the wanted set bit within that window, so the half
containing the target is always the one kept.

The window is `+value`, so 8- and 16-bit types are searched at 32 bits. The shift
amount is at most `digits / 2`, so no shift reaches the width of the type, including
the `__uint128_t` instantiation. All widths are driven by
`cuda::std::numeric_limits<T>::digits` rather than by type names, so platforms where
`unsigned long` is 32 bits behave the same as those where it is 64.

## Validation

Differential testing against an independent linear bit-scan oracle that shares no
logic with the binary search and does not use `popcount`:

- exhaustive over all `uint8_t` and `uint16_t` values (zero included) against every
  rank in `[0, num_bits)`, so every not-found rank is covered as well
- randomized `uint32_t`, `uint64_t` and `__uint128_t`
- about 9e7 checks in total, zero mismatches, and clean under UBSan

The committed test follows the structure of `bit_ffs.pass.cpp` and covers, in constant
evaluation and at run time:

- a `check(value)` helper that compares every rank in `[0, num_bits)` against a
  linear scan: the found ranks against the scanned positions, the remaining ranks
  against `-1`
- per type: a single set bit at every position, all-bits-set with every rank,
  `0b10110100` at ranks 0 to 4 with the last one not found, and `check` over zero,
  one, all ones, alternating bits, each half of the value, the two extremes and a
  pair straddling the first split, which for `__uint128_t` is bits 63 and 64
- API constraints: accepted for unsigned integer types, rejected for `bool`, signed
  integers, floating point and enumerations; `int` return type; `noexcept`

Toolchain, with nvcc 12.8.61 and gcc against cccl `main`:

- `-arch=sm_80`, `-arch=sm_90`, `-arch=sm_100`: compile clean
- `-std=c++17` and `-std=c++20`: compile clean
- `-DCCCL_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS`: compile clean
- `-Werror all-warnings`: clean
- the test's `main` was compiled directly with nvcc and executed on the host in each
  of those configurations, so both `assert(test())` and `static_assert(test())` ran
- `pre-commit run --files <the five files>`: all hooks pass

On an H200 (`sm_90`, driver 595.58, nvcc 12.8.61), with the exact commit pushed here:

- the committed test, compiled with `-arch=sm_90`, executed on the node at C++17,
  C++20 and C++20 with `CCCL_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS`
- the same `test()` body launched inside a kernel (it is `TEST_FUNC`, so host and
  device) in the same three configurations, with device-side asserts enabled: passes,
  no kernel error
- a device-side differential of the shipped header against a linear scan for every
  rank: all `uint8_t` and `uint16_t` values, plus 5.5e8 randomized values each for
  32, 64 and 128 bits, once with and once without `CCCL_ENABLE_ASSERTIONS`; 2.2e9
  checks per build, zero mismatches

What I could not run: the repository's own lit harness, plus the NVRTC, clang-cuda and
MSVC configurations of the CI matrix. I have nvcc + gcc on Linux, clang on macOS for
host-only probes, and a Hopper device; nothing Blackwell.

## Code generation

With nvcc 12.8.61 at `-O3`, using minimal one-call kernels; counts exclude `NOP`
alignment padding and subtract, per mnemonic, an otherwise identical kernel that
stores `i + r` instead of the call. That makes the absolute numbers approximate to
about plus or minus 2 (the baseline's one add is subtracted from every row, and the
early exit makes the compiler re-lower one address computation); the relative
comparison is unaffected:

| kernel | sm_90 | sm_100a | control flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| CUB `nth_set_bit` (no not-found handling) | 33 | 32 | none |
| `cuda::bit_fns<unsigned char>` | 28 | 27 | one early exit |
| `cuda::bit_fns<uint32_t>` | 41 | 40 | one early exit |
| `cuda::bit_fns<uint64_t>` | 53 | 52 | one early exit |
| `__fns` intrinsic | 54 | 54 | `BSSY` + 3 `BRA` + `BSYNC` |

Each search step lowers to predicated `SEL`s, so the loop itself is branch-free; the
only branch is the not-found early exit requested in review. `unsigned char` lands
below the 32-bit case because it runs log2(8) = 3 search steps instead of 5; promoting
its window to 32 bits does not change the step count.

The `sm_100a` column comes from cross-compiling the same kernels. `__fns` expands to
the same branchy sequence there, so it is not a native instruction on Blackwell
either. To be explicit: for Blackwell this is static inspection of the compiler
output only. I have no Blackwell device, so nothing was executed or timed there, and
every runtime number below is from an H200 (`sm_90`).

## Measurements

Method: every variant implements the same contract and is checked against a linear
scan for every rank in `[0, num_bits)` on device before timing; the rank comes from
the top bits of an independent LCG stream, so the timed region contains no modulo; an
identical kernel without the call is timed and subtracted; median of 5; a full-chip
launch (8 blocks of 256 threads per SM on all 132 SMs), reported as ps per call per
SM. Theoretical occupancy is register-limited: 75% for the `bit_fns` and bithacks
if-form/hybrid kernels (38 to 40 registers), 100% for `__fns`, the CUB helper and the
arithmetic-select form.

On the "potentially considering further optimizations" note in the issue, comparing
the alternatives at `uint32_t`. Every row in this table handles the not-found case
with a select after the search, so it compares the search algorithms themselves; the
shipped early-exit form is measured separately below:

| variant | ps/call/SM |
|---|---|
| `cuda::bit_fns` search, select-form not-found handling | 235 |
| `__fns` | 241 |
| bithacks SWAR select, if-form | 245 |
| bithacks, `POPC` for the two wide steps and SWAR for the tail | 261 |
| bithacks, published arithmetic select | 282 |

At 64 bits it is 304 for `bit_fns` (305 as shipped, with the early exit) against 388
for the bithacks form. The bithacks form wins on dependent-chain latency because its
partial sums are computed once up front: at 32 bits, 150 against 164 clocks when both
use a select after the search, 217 against 235 when both use the early exit as
shipped. It loses on throughput because it is more instructions: the SWAR ladder costs
more than the `POPC` it replaces. In an earlier single-warp screen against the plain
binary search, a byte-level first stage cost 34% more clocks per call, a two-level
4-ary search 93% more, and iterating `v &= v - 1` roughly 7x; none of those was
carried into the full-chip comparison.

On the early exit specifically, that is the shipped form against the select form in
the table: with ranks that always identify a set bit the two measure the same (238
against 238); with ranks where about half are not found, so the branch diverges, the
early exit costs about 2% (240 against 235). Both were verified against the linear
scan first.

Closes #11051

---

## Notes for review

- `_CCCL_PRAGMA_UNROLL_FULL()` is kept: the trip count is a compile-time constant, so
  the compiler should unroll the loop without it, but `popcount.h`, `byteswap.h` and
  `bit_repeat.h` use the pragma on the same kind of loop.
- The CUB call site is left in place. It clamps the rank into range before the call,
  so it has no use for a not-found result and adopting `bit_fns` there would make it
  pay for a check it does not need. Replacing it is a small follow-up, and worth
  measuring separately.
- No host BMI2 `PDEP` / Arm SVE2 `BDEP` specialization is included. Note that
  selecting the n-th set bit is the deposit operation, not the `PEXT` / `BEXT` named
  in the issue. It can follow separately if wanted.

items.title: Add warp-aggregated CUB block histogram algorithms
items.body:
## Summary

Adds a new `cub::BlockHistogram` algorithm that reduces same-bin atomic contention within each warp before updating the histogram:

- `cub::BLOCK_HISTO_ATOMIC_WARP_AGGREGATED`: uses warp match primitives and a leader lane to issue one atomic add per distinct bin value in the warp.

The implementation uses native `__match_any_sync` on SM70+ targets and falls back to CUB's `MatchAny` helper below SM70, including the partial-final-warp form when the block size is not a multiple of the hardware warp size.

This extends the existing block histogram Catch2 coverage to exercise the new algorithm, including a 33-thread partial-warp block case, and adds an nvbench benchmark for comparing `atomic`, `warp_aggregated`, and `sort` across item count, bin count, block count, and entropy.

## Benchmark Summary

I ran the full benchmark matrix from `cub.bench.block_histogram.algorithms.base` on:

- GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
- CMake build: Release
- CUDA architecture: `sm_120`
- Benchmark matrix: `ItemsPerThread={1,4,8}`, `Bins={32,128,2048}`, `Blocks={4096,16384}`, `Entropy={0.000,0.201,1.000}`

The benchmark data below is filtered to the remaining algorithms after dropping the cooperative-groups variant in PR feedback. The later SM70 guard keeps the benchmarked SM120 path on native match-any and adds the lower-target fallback path.

Across the 54 non-algorithm configurations:

- Fastest algorithm counts: `warp_aggregated` 48, `atomic` 6.
- `warp_aggregated` vs plain `atomic`: 42 wins, 8 near-neutral cases, 4 losses, geometric mean speedup 1.51x.
- Best speedup: 3.77x for `ItemsPerThread=8, Bins=32, Blocks=16384, Entropy=0.000`.
- The wins are largest when bin collisions are common. High-entropy / large-bin cases become neutral or slightly negative because the grouping overhead has fewer duplicate bin updates to amortize.

Representative `ItemsPerThread=8, Blocks=16384` GPU times:

| Bins | Entropy | atomic | warp_aggregated | Speedup | sort |
| ---: | ------: | -----: | ---------------: | ------: | ---: |
| 32 | 0.000 | 415.516 us | 110.345 us | 3.77x | 335.275 us |
| 128 | 0.000 | 379.250 us | 112.657 us | 3.37x | 335.871 us |
| 2048 | 0.000 | 398.879 us | 202.859 us | 1.97x | 362.679 us |
| 32 | 0.201 | 374.142 us | 110.545 us | 3.38x | 341.186 us |
| 128 | 0.201 | 338.694 us | 111.421 us | 3.04x | 339.838 us |
| 2048 | 0.201 | 357.340 us | 203.199 us | 1.76x | 368.558 us |
| 32 | 1.000 | 127.035 us | 111.175 us | 1.14x | 339.936 us |
| 128 | 1.000 | 173.452 us | 141.329 us | 1.23x | 339.978 us |
| 2048 | 1.000 | 288.329 us | 285.490 us | 1.01x | 371.171 us |

## Codegen Notes

I also inspected representative `sm_120` SASS for `ItemsPerThread=8, Bins=32`:

| Algorithm | Instructions | MATCH | VOTE | POPC | REDG.ADD |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `atomic` | 56 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 8 |
| `warp_aggregated` | 120 | 8 | 8 | 8 | 8 |

The plain atomic path does not appear to get compiler-generated histogram-style warp aggregation: it emits one `REDG.E.ADD` per item and no `MATCH`, `VOTE`, or `POPC` grouping sequence. The raw warp-aggregated path has one grouping sequence per item and guards the add so only the elected leader lane updates each same-bin peer group. That explains the large low-entropy wins.

## Validation

- `pre-commit run --files cub/cub/block/block_histogram.cuh cub/cub/block/specializations/block_histogram_atomic_warp_aggregated.cuh cub/test/catch2_test_block_histogram.cu cub/benchmarks/bench/block_histogram/algorithms.cu`
- `cmake --build build/cub-cpp20 --target cub.test.block.histogram`
- `ctest --test-dir build/cub-cpp20 -R '^cub\\.test\\.block\\.histogram' --output-on-failure` passed 3/3 tests
- `cmake --build build/cub-benchmark --target cub.bench.block_histogram.algorithms.base`
- `build/cub-benchmark/bin/cub.bench.block_histogram.algorithms.base --list` reports 162 configurations and algorithms `atomic`, `warp_aggregated`, and `sort`
- Full `cub.bench.block_histogram.algorithms.base` benchmark matrix on GPU 0
- `git diff --check`
- Local RoboRev branch code review against `origin/main`: no issues found
- Local RoboRev branch design review against `origin/main`: pass

Local CUDA 13 tooling only advertises `compute_75` and newer, so I could not run an actual pre-SM70 compile here. The lower-target path is guarded through `NV_IF_ELSE_TARGET` and uses CUB's existing `MatchAny` fallback.

items.title: [STF] data_place::replicated — one copy per grid member, read-only
items.body:
A replicated data place duplicates a logical data over the affine data places of an execution grid's members: one padded replica per place (stride = size rounded to the placement granularity), VA-contiguous so the instance exposes replica 0 and ordinary code paths see a normal device allocation.

Replication is a PLACEMENT property, not an access mode:
- copies INTO the place populate replica 0 and fan out to the others (stream: same-stream memcpys; graph: a chain of memcpy nodes whose tail carries the dependencies), and writes at the place are rejected at task creation -- so a valid replicated instance is synced by construction, with no new coherence state;
- each shard of a grid parallel_for reads its own replica: the dispatch rebases mdspan instances by place_index * stride (the stride helper is shared with the allocation path so the two cannot drift);
- mutation happens at any other place and invalidates the instance; the next replicated read re-broadcasts (ordinary MSI);
- allocations are recycled through the composite cache, so replicated instances inherit the stackable pop-time handover (#10609) and work inside conditional graph scopes.

The natural first customer is data-parallel training within a GPU (shared NN weights read by every locality domain), whose write-side dual -- per-place partial accumulators -- already exists as reduce() access modes.

Test: places/replicated_data_place.cu -- value correctness through a 2-place grid on the stream backend, the graph backend, and a repeat_graph_scope conditional loop; read-only enforcement; verified on sm_103 (existing stackable/cute suites pass unchanged).

items.title: [c.parallel.v2] hostjit: unregister the fatbin when a produced library is unloaded
items.body:
## Description

A library produced by the host JIT registers its fatbin with CUDART when it is loaded and never unregisters it. The registration glue schedules the unregister through `atexit`, and the produced library is freestanding: no C runtime, so no `__cxa_atexit` and no finalizer to run it. Closing the library unmaps the image while CUDART still holds a pointer into it, which is the crash analysed in [#9367](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/issues/9367).

That crash was worked around in [#9402](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cccl/pull/9402) by not closing a JIT module at all, which trades it for a leak: every module ever compiled stays mapped and registered for the life of the process, and its device memory with it. This supplies the missing unregister, so the modules can be closed again.

### What this does

The `atexit` that stands in for the C library's in the freestanding compilation keeps the one registration the CUDA registration constructor makes -- the module destructor, which unregisters the fatbin -- and the produced library makes that call when it is unloaded, through the hook its platform offers: a `.fini_array` entry on ELF, the DLL's entry point on Windows, named on the link line with `/ENTRY:__hostjit_dll_entry`. The image also exports two functions, for a loader that wants the teardown to happen before the unmap: `__cudacc_module_fini`, which makes that call, and `__cudacc_module_sync`, which calls `cudaDeviceSynchronize` in whichever cudart the image is bound to.

It is not a C library's `atexit` and does not try to be one. There is no table and no process-exit behaviour: a freestanding image has no C runtime to hold a list of callbacks until the process ends, and the name exists here only because the registration constructor's call has to land somewhere. So it takes that one registration and refuses everything else, and a program that asks for the same hook does not compile. Two things ask for it. A written call to `atexit`, which the header the host translation units force-include renames to a declaration marked unavailable; and an object whose destructor has to run at exit, which never names `atexit` at all -- for the MSVC ABI the compiler emits that very call for it, for a namespace-scope global as much as for a function-local static -- and which `-Werror=exit-time-destructors` refuses. That one goes to every host compilation, a precompiled header included: a header is built by one call and the code emitted by another, and the second does not diagnose again what it read from the first. Either way the refusal arrives where the program is built rather than through a return value at run time, which the compiler's own registration does not read either. glibc's equivalent tags every entry with the library that registered it, through `__cxa_atexit`, so `__cxa_finalize` can run that library's own at `dlclose`; here there is one entry and one image, and nothing to tag.

What a C library does not have to deal with is the unmap. An exit handler returns and the memory goes, whereas this image cannot be unmapped until the device has finished with it and CUDART has dropped its pointer into it. That wait cannot be done from the finalizer, which the loader calls with its lock held, which is why the image exports the two entry points instead of only unregistering as it is closed.

All of that is one object that `libnvccLinkToSharedLibrary` compiles and adds to every link, the way a C runtime contributes its own startup and teardown object. One definition per library is what lets it be a strong one, so an object that defines `atexit` too fails the link instead of quietly taking the registration constructor's call.

`libnvccLinkToSharedLibrary` takes one object, since each object carries its own fatbin and registers it at load, so a second one would mean two registrations for one body of code. It also refuses an output library whose directory has a `%` in its name: the linker's atomic write takes a `%` as a placeholder wherever in the path it sits, so one in a directory name sends the temporary file it writes to a directory that does not exist. A `%` in the library's own file name is fine, reaching that temporary name only.

### What a caller sees

`dlopen` and `dlclose`, or `LoadLibrary` and `FreeLibrary`, and nothing else. The artifact is self-contained: the fatbin is registered when the image is opened and unregistered when it is closed, by code inside the image. It has to be, because the artifact is not always opened by the JIT that built it — in the ahead-of-time case it is compiled once and opened later from a process that never linked the JIT.

Read on Linux, a produced library needs `libcudart` and nothing else, and its undefined symbols are ten cudart entry points. Two holders of one library work: a second `dlopen` bumps a reference count without re-running the constructors, and the finalizer runs when the last handle goes, so the fatbin is registered once and unregistered once.

### When the memory comes back

Unregistering does not unload anything by itself. `__cudaUnregisterFatBinary` drops the host-side entries and moves a module the driver has already loaded into a pending-unload set; the driver-side unload is issued from the next runtime call. So after a plain `dlclose` the device state comes back at whatever the process does next with CUDA, and an application that goes quiet keeps it resident. The image cannot force it: its finalizer runs on the loader lock. A CUDART entry point for that flush is the durable answer and does not exist today.

A caller that needs the state back at a known point drives the teardown itself, which is what `DynamicLibrary::unload()` does: wait for the module's work, `__cudacc_module_fini`, one more wait to push the queued unload out, then unmap. Both waits go through the image's own `__cudacc_module_sync`, so they land in the cudart the module registered with — a process can hold more than one, each with its own module registry and pending-unload queue.

A wait that did not happen stops the unload. `cudaDeviceSynchronize` refuses outright while the calling thread is capturing a stream, so work from the module may still be running, and `unload()` reports the failure and keeps the module rather than unmapping it under a kernel. The failure is handed back rather than left behind: the wait clears it in the runtime it called, which a caller with a runtime of its own cannot reach, and where it would otherwise be waiting to come back from the module's next launch. The two waits do not leave the same state behind: before the teardown the module is untouched, after it the fatbin is unregistered and the unmap is safe to make, so what a failure there costs is the device state, not the module's safety, and a later call resumes from the wait that failed instead of repeating the sequence. Whoever owns the module keeps it for that retry — the twelve `cccl_device_*_cleanup` entry points return `CUDA_ERROR_ILLEGAL_STATE` and keep the compiler and the payload the retry needs, clearing the launch pointer alone, since by then the fatbin may already be unregistered and there is nothing left to launch. `DynamicLibrary`'s move assignment swaps the two states instead of dropping the handle. `cudaErrorCudartUnloading` is not treated as a failure: the runtime is going down with the process, so both waits are pointless, while the teardown still runs here rather than from the finalizer during the unmap.

An image that does not export the two entry points is refused at load, naming the one that is missing, and left mapped: loading it has run its constructors, so closing it would strand the registration it has already made.

### What is guaranteed

A produced shared library can be loaded and unloaded repeatedly without leaking memory or accumulating state in the driver, with the one qualification above about when the driver-side unload is issued.

### Tests

- `test_hostjit_unload` — the engine-driven path: wait, unregister, flush, unmap, with free device memory back at the level it had before the load, read through the driver so that a module released only because the runtime was called again does not pass. It also covers what the sequence has to survive: a module dropped with a kernel still running, an unload refused from inside a stream capture, an image this compiler did not produce, and the three ways a program asks for the image's exit hook, none of which compile.
- `test_libnvcc_artifact_unload` — the artifact on its own, built through the library API and then opened and closed with plain `dlopen` and `dlclose` from a process that knows nothing of the teardown sequence. Removing the `.fini_array` entry leaves 16 MiB gone and fails it. It also covers the refused links, and the object the link writes into the caller's directory for the teardown: files planted there beforehand keep their content, and nothing of the link's own is left behind.
- `test_hostjit_unload_shared_image` — pins what `DynamicLibrary` does with two handles on one image, so that a later change is noticed.
- `test.reduce` — the refusal as the C API shows it: `cccl_device_reduce_cleanup` reports it, drops the launch pointer, keeps the rest, and a second call finishes the unload. A module built before the refusal then runs, which is what shows the refused wait left no error behind in the runtime the modules share.

### Known limitations

- `atexit` in the compiled program, and with it any object whose destructor has to run at exit. Not available here: the image's one exit hook belongs to the fatbin unregister, and a program asking for it is refused while it compiles. Running a program's callback at unload is a separate mechanism, which a compiler that emits the unregister without going through `atexit` would leave room for.
- A wait refused after the unregister. `unload()` reports it and a later call resumes from there, and nothing in the suite arranges that state any more. Other things can put it there -- concurrent work of the caller's failing in between the two waits, among them -- but not at a point a test can name; what is gone is the deterministic way the test had, a callback of the program's beginning a stream capture between the two.
- Linking several CUDA objects into one library. It did not work before either, the `atexit` stub this replaces being defined per translation unit, so two host objects failed at link on a duplicate symbol. Relocatable device compilation generates the registration once at the final link and is what lifts the restriction; enabling it is a follow-up change.
- Closing an artifact by hand with a kernel still in flight. The hook in the image runs under the loader lock, so it unregisters and returns without waiting; a caller that closes an artifact itself has to synchronize first.
- Concurrent use during the unload. The waits cover GPU work, not the host side: a pointer taken from the image stays callable until the unmap. The caller has to have stopped using the module before unloading it, which is the contract `dlclose` comes with as well.
- Unloading a module whose kernels run on a device other than the caller's current one. The wait covers the current device, so the contract is to unload from the thread and device that used the module; covering every device would create a CUDA context on devices the process never touched.
- What the registration on Windows costs. The fatbin is registered from the attach path of the DLL's entry point, which the loader calls with its own lock held. An ordinary DLL with a C runtime registers from the same place, so this is not a new position to be in, but neither the time it takes nor the risk of re-entering the loader has been measured.
- The early sequence on an image that two `DynamicLibrary` objects opened. It asks the image to tear down without asking whether anyone else holds it, so the first unload unregisters the fatbin and the second holder is left with a library it can no longer launch from. Plain `dlclose` does not have this problem, because the OS counts the holders. `test_hostjit_unload_shared_image` pins that behaviour, so the scenario is watched rather than untested; what is missing is holder counting, which needs either a count in the image or a registration the runtime counts.

items.title: [FEA]: Determine the best approach of tuning the Segmented Algorithms with regard to their segment size

type.name: Enhancement
type.description: A request, idea, or new functionality

items.body:
### Area

CUB

### Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

The family of segmented algorithms in CCCL (e.g., segmented sort, segmented radix sort) suffers from an inherent tuning problem:

Any new tuning configuration inevitably speeds up one class of segment sizes while causing regressions in others.

This happens because the performance characteristics of small, medium, and large segments differ so much that no single tuning or heuristic applies well to all of them. Because of that:

- small segments prefer low-overhead, fine-grained kernels,
- large segments prefer aggressive caching, large CTAs, and high throughput,
- mid-range segments break when the bucket boundaries shift.

This structural imbalance makes **segmented algorithms extremely sensitive to tuning**, and changes almost always introduce regressions in a class of segment sizes. Any change to tuning(_bucket boundaries, CTA sizes, memory tiling, policies_) inevitably optimizes one segment-size regime and harms another.

Finally, **the heuristic that decides bucket boundaries is critical**. If segmented sizes are known _a priori_  tuning values can be selected accordingly and significantly improve performance, because the algorithm will not have to traverse throughout all segments to figure out which kernel to invoke for each.

---

TL;DR

The core issue with CCCL segmented algorithms is the structural tuning conflict caused by segment size variance.

- Segment size knowledge is the fundamental bottleneck for applying cohesive tunings throughout the segmented algorithm.
- Bucket heuristics amplify the tradeoff.
- User-defined tuning policies (when enabled) will be a reliable solution but will still require effort from the user.

---

TODO

Given that segmented algorithms cannot be tuned globally across the full set of their workloads, find out

- [ ] which workloads are more representative
- [ ] how can we prioritize best within the segmented algorithms workloads (is there a class of segments size that is more important than others?)

items.title: Adds `thrust::erase` and `thrust::erase_if`
items.body:
## Description

closes #727

Adds `thrust::erase` and `thrust::erase_if` for `thrust::host_vector` and `thrust::device_vector`, following the C++20 container erasure idiom (`std::erase`/`std::erase_if`) and eliminating the need for the manual erase-remove idiom.

Both functions are implemented as host-only APIs, since resizing a vector requires host-side allocator and destructor calls that cannot be expressed as device code:

- `erase(c, value)` removes all elements equal to `value` from vector `c` and returns the number of elements removed.
- `erase_if(c, pred)` removes all elements from vector `c` for which the predicate `pred` returns `true`, and returns the number of elements removed.

Both are also available as overloads accepting an execution policy, e.g. `thrust::erase(thrust::cuda::par.on(stream), c, value)`. The supplied execution policy is applied to the underlying stream compaction step (`thrust::remove`/`thrust::remove_if`); the subsequent container resize is performed host-side via `Vector::erase`.

A new type trait `is_thrust_vector_v<T>` was introduced to constrain these overloads to `thrust::host_vector` and `thrust::device_vector`.

Note: unlike `remove`/`remove_if`, `erase`/`erase_if` compare/test elements against the container's `value_type` directly (no implicit cast of the comparison value), matching `std::erase`'s semantics. `U` (the type of the value passed to `erase`) only needs to be comparable to `Vector::value_type` via `operator==`, not implicitly convertible to it.

### Testing
- Correctness tests for `erase`/`erase_if` covering empty vectors, single/multiple/all/no matches, consecutive and alternating matches, first/last element, and large vectors (10000 elements), for both `host_vector` and `device_vector` across `NumericTypes`.
- CUDA stream tests verifying `erase`/`erase_if` work correctly with a custom `cudaStream_t` via `thrust::cuda::par.on(s)`, including a non-trivially-destructible element type.
- A dedicated test covering the heterogeneous-type comparison path (`U != value_type`).

* I didn't add an example but I can submit it later if desired
* I didn't add benchmark tests since the implementation relies on the `thrust::remove`/`thrust::remove_if` implementation which is already benchmarked

items.body:
## Description closes #9077 #9259 #9548 # Cluster-based Segmented Top-K (CUB) This PR adds a **thread-block-cluster** implementation of segmented top-k to CUB and **unifies it with the existing baseline backend** behind CUB's public `cub::DeviceBatchedTopK` API. Given `num_segments` segments, each of variable size, the algorithm selects the `k` largest (or smallest) keys of every segment (optionally carrying a value payload, i.e. key/value pairs). This is a **production backend**, not a throwaway prototype. `cub::DeviceBatchedTopK` now exposes two backends behind **one kernel symbol** and picks between them per architecture (the compile-time, device-side `policy_selector_from_types`, resolved via `current_policy` + `if constexpr`): - **baseline** — the pre-existing *worker-per-segment* backend (one thread block per segment). It serves segments that fit a single thread block on **all** architectures, but currently only the fully non-deterministic request `(not_guaranteed, unspecified)`. - **cluster** — this PR's backend, for **SM 9.0+**. It handles segments too large for a single block and every supported determinism / tie-break combination. The backend is chosen from three request facts: the **architecture**, the **statically-known maximum segment size**, and the **determinism / tie-break** requirement. Deterministic (or tie-broken) requests, and segments larger than the baseline can cover, route to the cluster backend (SM 9.0+); among non-deterministic, baseline-coverable requests the baseline-vs-cluster choice is an architecture / segment-size crossover. When no backend can serve the request on a target architecture the dispatch reports it either at compile time (strict, default) or at runtime as `cudaErrorNotSupported` (see §3.6, §10). Because this is **CUB's first cluster kernel**, this document spends extra time on the cluster-specific mechanics — distributed shared memory, cluster barriers (and how few of them we use), the leader block, dynamic cluster sizing, and portability — which reviewers will not have seen elsewhere in the codebase. --- ## 1. High-level overview
One cluster per segment · radix digit top-k · histogram merge · early stop · output placement · determinism ### 1.1 One cluster per segment, sized for portability The kernel launches a grid of **thread-block clusters** and assigns **exactly one cluster to one segment**. The blocks (CTAs) of a cluster co-operate through *distributed shared memory* (DSMEM) and *cluster barriers*, so a segment is processed entirely on-chip without a global scratch buffer or multiple kernel launches. (The non-segmented `cub::DeviceTopK` instead uses a multi-kernel + global-histogram pipeline; the baseline worker-per-segment backend keeps each segment within a single block.) The number of CTAs per cluster (the "cluster width") is chosen **at runtime** by the dispatch layer, so it is *not* a template parameter; the agent reads it from `cooperative_groups::this_cluster().num_blocks()`. The primary reason to spread a segment across a runtime-sized cluster (rather than baking in a fixed size) is **portability**: the resident shared-memory budget that lets a segment of a given size stay on-chip is not guaranteed on future GPUs, so we size the cluster to whatever the device actually offers. Being able to feed the runtime maximum-segment-size information into the dispatch decision is a welcome bonus, but not the main motivation. For the same reason the resident key storage lives in **dynamic** shared memory (Section 3.2) rather than a compile-time-sized static buffer. ### 1.2 Radix (digit) top-k Selection uses the standard **multi-pass radix / digit-iteration** approach shared with the rest of CUB's top-k (`detail::topk`): process the key one `bits_per_pass`-bit digit at a time, from the most-significant digit down. Each pass: 1. Builds a histogram over the current digit, restricted to *candidate* keys (keys whose higher digits already match the running "k-th key" prefix). 2. Finds the bucket that contains the k-th element and narrows `k` and the candidate set to that bucket. 3. Sets the winning digit in a running splitter key. After the passes converge, the *splitter key* (the k-th largest key) is known, and a **final filter pass** writes out: - every key **strictly** above the splitter (the "front"), plus - exactly enough keys **equal** to the splitter (the "back"/tie region) to reach `k`. ```mermaid flowchart LR P0["Pass 0 (MSD digit)
candidates = all keys"] --> P1["Pass 1
candidates = k-th bucket"] P1 --> P2["Pass 2
candidate set shrinks"] P2 --> Pn["Pass n (LSD digit)
splitter (k-th key) known"] Pn --> F["final filter
front (> splitter) + back (= splitter)"] P1 -. "bucket holds exactly k → early stop" .-> F ``` ### 1.3 The histogram: block-private accumulation + DSMEM merge into the leader Each pass builds the cluster-wide histogram in three steps: 1. **Block-private accumulation.** Every CTA lays out `hist[num_buckets]` at the *same* offset in its own shared memory and accumulates its own keys into it with the builtin shared-memory `atomicAdd`. 2. **DSMEM merge into the leader.** Every non-leader CTA walks its local histogram and reduces each nonzero bucket into the **leader** CTA's `hist` through DSMEM. The leader's `hist` therefore does double duty: its own block-private histogram first, then the cluster-merged histogram after the merge. 3. **Splitter identification.** The leader's threads prefix-sum the merged histogram (`cub::BlockScan`), find the bucket holding the k-th key, and publish the result into a cluster-shared `state`. Every CTA reads that result back and sets the winning digit in its *own* local splitter key (so the full splitter key never has to be broadcast). ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph bp["1 · block-private accumulation"] A["CTA 0
local hist"] B["CTA 1

local hist"] end L["leader CTA hist
(own hist, then merged hist)"] A -- "2 · DSMEM reduce" --> L B -- "2 · DSMEM reduce" --> L C -- "2 · DSMEM reduce" --> L L --> S["3 · BlockScan merged hist
find k-th bucket"] S --> R["publish pass_result
(kth_bucket, early_stop)"] R -. "read back via DSMEM,
set digit in own splitter" .-> A R -.-> B R -.-> C ``` ### 1.4 Early stop When the identified splitter bucket contains *exactly* the remaining `k` candidates, every candidate in it is part of the answer and no finer digit can change the result. The leader sets an `early_stop` flag; every CTA decodes it from the same broadcast word and breaks out of the pass loop together. ### 1.5 Final filter and output placement The final pass re-reads the segment's keys and routes each through **one shared placement helper** (`place_one`): the front (strictly-selected) and back (tie) paths are **unified** — a single block-local SMEM `atomicAdd` on the relevant region counter yields the key's output slot, and a uniform `out < k` guard drops the losing ties while always accepting a strictly-selected key. Both regions fill **forward** (low index up): - **Front** (strictly above the splitter) → the front region `[0, num_selected)`. - **Back** (ties equal to the splitter) → the back region `[num_selected, k)` (i.e. `[k - num_ties, k)`). The trick is that the two region counters are **pre-seeded to this CTA's absolute region base**, so the placing `atomicAdd` returns the final output slot with no per-key base arithmetic. Computing those bases is the one cross-CTA step, done by a **cross-CTA prefix scan**: a handful of one-time cross-CTA pushes seed every CTA's front and back counters to their region bases at once (Section 2.5), after which per-element placement is just the bare block-local SMEM `atomicAdd` above, fully decoupling the CTAs (no shared cursor). (An earlier design instead kept a **DSMEM output cursor**: each output element claimed its slot with a fetch-add into a cluster-wide cursor held in the leader via DSMEM atomics — one DSMEM atomic per placed key. Section 2.5 keeps the comparison because it explains *why* the scan is the better shape.) The scan puts its (single) cluster barrier *before* the filter (a post-push sync), so there is **no cluster barrier after the final filter pass** and CTAs exit independently — unlike the old DSMEM cursor, which needed a cluster barrier *after* the filter (whose later timing also gated early exit). ```text Output array (length k): 0 k-1 |<------------- front region --------------->|<--- back / ties --->| [ keys strictly > splitter, packed by CTA ][ keys == splitter ] ^ ^ k - num_ties k both regions fill forward; each CTA's front/back counters are pre-seeded to its region base by the cross-CTA scan ``` ### 1.6 Determinism / tie-breaking The public request carries a `cuda::execution::determinism` requirement and an optional `tie_break` preference: - **Non-deterministic** (default): both front and back use racing shared-memory atomics; among equal (tied) keys, *which* ones land in the back is arrival-order (nondeterministic), but the *set* of winning keys is always correct. - **Deterministic**: the back region is filled in **segment-index order** via an index-ordered `BlockScan`, so a reproducible subset of the tied keys wins. `prefer_larger_index` reverses the scan so the largest-index ties win instead of the smallest. The determinism contract is that the **set** of winning elements is deterministic, not their output positions. The user can also request weaker, valid intermediate points on the determinism / tie-break lattice (e.g. run-to-run determinism, or GPU-to-GPU determinism with an unspecified tie-break). For now those all **map onto** the two behaviors above, because we do not yet know a cheaper way to provide them.
--- ## 2. Cluster mechanics (the first-cluster-kernel details)
Cluster barriers · DSMEM and state · leader and pass_result · idle ranks · cross-CTA output scan This is the section most worth close review, since these patterns are new to CUB. ### 2.1 Cluster barriers and how we minimize them A cluster barrier (`cluster.sync()`) is **expensive**: unlike `__syncthreads()`, synchronizing across CTAs generally requires a round-trip through L2. Keeping their count low is a first-order concern, so several design choices exist purely to avoid cluster barriers: - **Front-load all local shared-memory initialization before the first cluster barrier.** Every counter the later phases rely on (histogram, the output-scan accumulator, the local front/back counters, the `state` fields) is zeroed *before* the launch's first `cluster.sync()`, so that one cluster barrier both orders the inits and publishes them cluster-wide. No later phase needs its own extra init-ordering cluster barrier. - **No cluster barrier between the block-private histogram and the merge.** Naively, all CTAs would need a cluster barrier after building their local histograms before reducing them into the leader (so the leader's own local increments are ordered ahead of the incoming reductions). We drop that cluster barrier by leaning on atomic scope instead: the block-private increments use the builtin `atomicAdd`, whose default `.gpu` scope already spans the cluster peers, so the leader's own increments are mutually atomic with the non-leaders' `.cluster`-scoped DSMEM reductions racing into the same `hist`. That saves one L2-round-trip cluster barrier per pass. (See §6 for why the local `atomicAdd` still needs a pinned 32-bit shared base to stay cheap.) - **The cross-CTA output scan needs only one cluster barrier.** Because the front/back placement counters (`front_local_cnt`/`back_local_cnt`) are pre-zeroed with the front-loaded inits above, the scan is a set of fire-and-forget pushes followed by a **single** post-push cluster barrier — there is no separate "start of scan" cluster barrier. (This is the only cluster barrier the scan adds; earlier notes about a "cluster-prefix barrier" refer to exactly this one post-push cluster barrier.) - **No cluster barrier after the final filter pass.** The last cluster barrier is the post-push scan barrier that *precedes* the filter; the filter itself writes output through block-local atomics into gmem, touching no peer, so the last cross-CTA access is the already-fenced output-seeding step. Every value a CTA still needs from a peer afterward (notably the leader's `early_stop`) is **cached into registers before that last cluster barrier**, so no CTA reads a peer's shared memory during or after the filter and each can return independently. This co-residency safety matters: reading a peer that has already returned faults the launch ("cluster target block not present"). *(This exact shape may change if the output seeding changes; see Section 2.5.)* The net per-pass cost is small: a local `__syncthreads()` plus **two** cluster barriers (one before the leader reads the merged histogram, one that publishes the pass result / orders the histogram reset), and one post-push cluster barrier for the output scan. A single-CTA "cluster" (Section 3.4) has no peers, so `cluster_or_block_sync(single_cta)` routes every one of these cluster barriers to a plain `__syncthreads()` and all atomics drop to CTA scope. ### 2.2 Distributed shared memory (DSMEM) and `state` Every CTA allocates the identical `_TempStorage` layout, so any field can be reached in a peer CTA at a known offset. Cross-CTA reads/writes are done through DSMEM (a CTA's shared memory mapped into another rank's address space); the histogram merge and the output scan write into a peer's fields, and the leader's `state` is read back by every CTA. The cluster-shared `state` (type `state_t`, nested in the agent so its counters reuse the kernel's 32-bit `offset_t`/`out_offset_t`) lives in the **leader** block's shared memory. It is split into two naturally-aligned 8-byte sub-structs — `size {len, k}` and `result {kth_bucket, early_stop}` (§2.3) — so each is fetched with a single DSMEM load. Non-leaders have no local copy; they read it from the leader through DSMEM (and cache what they need). ### 2.3 The leader block and the `pass_result` broadcast One CTA is the **leader**. It owns the merged histogram and the shared `state`, does the `BlockScan`-based splitter identification, and publishes the per-pass result. The per-pass result is an 8-byte `pass_result` sub-struct with two `uint32_t` fields: - `kth_bucket`: the splitter bucket (each CTA sets this digit in its own splitter key); - `early_stop`: the early-stop flag. Because the sub-struct is exactly 8 bytes and naturally aligned, every CTA pulls it from the leader with a **single 64-bit DSMEM load** (`ld.shared::cluster.u64`) via the templated `leader_state_load` accessor, which `cuda::std::bit_cast`s the loaded word back to the sub-struct and decodes both halves locally — no second remote load for the early-stop check, and no broadcast of the full splitter key. (The `size {len, k}` sub-struct is read the same way. An earlier version hand-packed the two halves into a `uint64_t` with shifts/masks and forced 16-byte state alignment; the two 8-byte sub-structs drop both the manual packing and the over-alignment.) The leader is always the CTA that is **last** in the cross-CTA scan order. This is required, not arbitrary: the leader's histogram has been *merged with everyone else's*, so it cannot recover its own local front/candidate counts directly. Sitting last in the scan, it receives the sum over all other CTAs and derives its own counts by subtracting that sum from the known totals. (For the deterministic-prefer-smaller case "last" is the highest effective rank; otherwise it is rank 0.) ### 2.4 Idle ranks The launch is sized for the *largest* segment a cluster may have to handle, so a smaller segment may not have enough chunks to give every CTA of its cluster work. Those CTAs are **idle ranks**: they own no chunks, contribute nothing, and never lead. They cannot simply return, because they still have to arrive at every `cluster.sync()` — a CTA that returned early would make the cluster barrier unreachable and hang the cluster. Each cluster-barrier site notes (`TODO(cccl)`) that a sub-cluster mbarrier over just the working ranks would let idle ranks exit and free their SM slots (see Section 10). ### 2.5 Seeding output positions: the cross-CTA scan (and the cursor it replaced) Output positions are seeded through **DSMEM atomics**. The chosen design is a cross-CTA scan; an earlier DSMEM output cursor is contrasted throughout because the contrast is exactly what motivates the scan: *how many* atomics (cluster-bounded and paid once vs. one per placed element), whether they are fire-and-forget or fetch-add, and — consequently — where the cross-CTA cluster barrier lands. As introduced in Section 1.5, each CTA needs its front/back region bases. The chosen design is a **cross-CTA prefix scan fused with priming the placement counters** (`prime_placement_counters`): each CTA adds its selected count and its candidate count into every successor's `front_local_cnt` and `back_local_cnt` — the very counters the final filter later places into. The same call also adds this CTA's own back-region base `num_selected` into its own `back_local_cnt`, so after the scan the counters already hold the **absolute region bases** the filter needs: `front_local_cnt = sel_prefix` and `back_local_cnt = num_selected + cand_prefix`. The leader is last, so it ends up holding the full predecessor sum and derives its own counts by subtraction. As a bonus, after the scan every CTA also knows the totals it needs for the early-exit bookkeeping without any further DSMEM traffic. **Two 32-bit pushes, not one 64-bit push.** An earlier version packed both counts into a single `(front_count << 32) | cand_count` word and scanned them with one 64-bit add. That was dropped because `red.add.u64` on **shared** memory is not a native atomic — ptxas emulates it with a CAS-spin loop (`ATOMS.CAST.SPIN.64` in SASS) — whereas two `red.add.u32`s are native warp-aggregatable shared atomics. So each CTA now issues **two independent 32-bit DSMEM reductions** per successor (front lane and back lane); they were never going to carry into each other anyway. ```text Every rank adds its counts into all higher ranks via DSMEM atomics — fire-and-forget, all in parallel: from \ into │ r1 r2 r3 = leader ─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────── r0 (c0) │ c0 c0 c0 r1 (c1) │ · c1 c1 r2 (c2) │ · · c2 ─────────────┼───────────────────────────────────── prefix held │ c0 c0+c1 c0+c1+c2 ← leader; own = totals − sum (cₓ = one CTA's counts, pushed as two 32-bit red.add.u32 — front lane + back lane — per cell) ``` These pushes are **fire-and-forget** atomics (they do not return a value), so, unlike a fetch-add into a shared cursor, they don't force a CTA-to-CTA round-trip to read a result back. They are also **lane-parallel** (each thread owns a strided slice of the successor ranks), which measurably beat the original single-threaded loop. Crucially, the scan's DSMEM traffic is **bounded by the cluster width and paid once** (O(cluster²) pushes), *independent of `k`* — the per-element placement that follows uses only cheap block-local SMEM atomics. The shared cursor instead issues **one DSMEM fetch-add per placed element**, so its cross-CTA atomic count scales with the number of placed keys: normally ≈ `k`, which is usually **≫ cluster width**, and it can even exceed `k` when candidates are placed before the CTA has observed early exit. (In the rare `k < cluster_size` regime the cursor could issue fewer, so this is a "typically", not a guarantee.) The two schemes also differ in **where the cross-CTA cluster barrier lands**, not whether one exists: the scan's cluster barrier sits *before* the filter (a post-push sync), so there is **no cluster barrier after the final filter pass** and CTAs exit independently; the old shared cursor instead needed a cluster barrier *after* the filter, whose later timing was precisely what **stopped CTAs from early-exiting**. The front-loaded inits (Section 2.1) hold either way.
